name: Constructive rest position

card.summary: Lying on the back with knees bent and feet flat to let the back and neck muscles release, used as a posture-awareness practice.
card.note: Spinal-decompression claims in popular guides are not backed by published trials.

quick.overview:
The constructive rest position is lying on the back with the knees bent and the feet flat on the floor, usually with a small book under the head. Practitioners, especially in the Alexander Technique and dance education, use it to let habitual muscle tension in the back and neck release, which they associate with easier, more upright posture.

Posture is part of how a person looks, so people in posture-focused circles use the position as a daily reset. Published trials on the position itself are lacking, and the research that exists concerns the Alexander Technique more broadly.
quick.how: People lie on a firm surface for a few minutes, once or twice a day by some guides, while directing attention to letting the back lengthen and widen. Advice on duration varies between sources, from a few minutes to fifteen or twenty. It is often done before or after training or at the end of a day.
quick.risks: It is a gentle, low-risk resting position. Anyone with a back or neck condition, or who cannot lie flat comfortably, may use variations; claims in popular guides about spinal discs rehydrating or posture changing lastingly are unsourced.

lead: Constructive rest, also called the semi-supine position or the balanced resting state, is a lying-down posture with the knees bent and the feet flat, associated with the Alexander Technique.[1] Guides describe it as a way to ease the spine and release habitual tension by working with gravity.

People who care about posture use it as a short daily practice, reasoning that less muscular holding in the back and neck leads to a more relaxed, upright stance when standing. One mailing-list contributor credits the position to Lulu Sweigard, while an Alexander Technique site says it grew from lying-down work F. M. Alexander developed.

Research on the position itself is lacking. The Alexander Technique more widely has been studied: the UK NHS and NICE cite evidence it may help long-term back and neck pain, while other reviews found limited or inconclusive evidence for posture and other outcomes.[1]

chain: Lying with knees bent unloads the spine against the floor

Easier, more upright standing posture over time
angle.text: Practitioners use the position to reduce muscular tension that shapes how they stand. The posture change is the claimed route to a taller, more open appearance.

paras: The position is lying on the back with knees up and feet on the floor. Guides present it as a foundational Alexander Technique practice for releasing habitual tension, and describe giving oneself mental directions while lying there.

The Alexander Technique was developed by F. M. Alexander (1869-1955), an actor who began working on it in the 1890s to address voice loss while performing.[1] An Alexander Technique site says the lying-down work later proved helpful even for people not taking lessons, and a mailing-list post credits Lulu Sweigard with the specific position.

The NHS and NICE cite evidence the Alexander Technique may help long-term back and neck pain; a 2012 Cochrane review found no good evidence for asthma, a 2014 review found inconclusive effects on musicians' posture and breathing, and a 2015 Australian review found limited evidence and little safety data.[1]
